Lore means a body of knowledge — a rich collection of stories, beliefs, traditions, and wisdom — about a particular subject, place, or group of people. It is knowledge that has been built up and passed down over time, often informally, through culture, storytelling, and shared experience rather than through textbooks or official sources.

Think of it as the accumulated wisdom and stories that a community, culture, or fandom holds about something.

Not all knowledge is lore. Lore has specific qualities that set it apart:

1. It belongs to a group or domain.
Lore is never just one person's private knowledge. It belongs to a community — a culture, a civilization, a fandom, a profession, or even a small village. It is shared knowledge. You speak of "the lore of the Scottish Highlands" or "the lore of the sea" — meaning the knowledge held collectively by those people or within that world.

2. It is passed down, not looked up.
Lore is traditionally handed from one generation to the next through stories, oral tradition, customs, and lived experience. A grandfather teaching his grandchildren which plants in the forest are poisonous and which are healing is passing down lore. It has a sense of being time-tested and inherited, not recently discovered or invented.

3. It blends fact, belief, and story.
This is crucial. Lore doesn't have to be 100% verifiable fact. It is a mixture of real knowledge, legend, myth, belief, and tradition. For example, "local lore" about a haunted house in a village might not be factually true, but it is still lore — because it is the story that people in that community have long believed and told. Lore lives in that fascinating space between history and mythology.

4. It has depth and richness.
Lore is never thin. The word implies a vast, layered collection of knowledge — not just a single fact or story, but an entire world of interconnected stories, rules, histories, and beliefs. When someone says a fictional universe has "deep lore," they mean it has a richly detailed internal history and mythology.

1. Cultural and folk lore
This is the oldest and most traditional use. Every human culture has its lore — the stories, myths, superstitions, customs, and ancient wisdom of its people.

"The lore of the Norse people was filled with gods, giants, and tales of the end of the world."
"According to local lore, the river would flood whenever the old willow tree bloomed early."

2. Nature and specialist lore
Lore also refers to specialized, practical knowledge about a subject — particularly nature — built up over long experience. Hunters, sailors, farmers, and herbalists all have their own lore.

"He knew the woodland lore well — how to track animals, read the weather by the clouds, and find water in dry land."
"Sea lore warned sailors never to whistle on a ship, as it was said to call up storms."

3. Fictional and fantasy lore
In modern usage — especially in gaming, fantasy, and science fiction — lore refers to the entire internal history, mythology, rules, and backstory of a fictional world. This is now one of the most common uses of the word.

"The lore of Middle-earth, built by Tolkien, spans thousands of years of fictional history."
"Players spent hours reading through the game's lore to understand why the kingdom had fallen."

These words are related but not the same:

  • Myth — A single story, usually about gods or the origins of the world. Lore is the entire collection of myths (and much more) belonging to a culture or world.
  • Legend — A single traditional story, often about a hero or a historical event that may be exaggerated. Again, lore is the whole body of such material.
  • Folklore — Very close to lore, and sometimes used interchangeably. Folklore is the academic term for the traditional stories, customs, and beliefs of a people. "Lore" is often used as a shorter, more literary version of this idea — but lore can also extend to specialist or fictional knowledge, where "folklore" would feel out of place.
  • History — Formal, documented, fact-based record of past events. Lore is more informal, oral, and emotionally and culturally rich. History is recorded; lore is remembered and felt.
  • Knowledge — A neutral, general word for anything known. Lore is a very specific kind of knowledge: inherited, cultural, story-rich, and often blending fact with belief.
The Feel and Tone of the Word

Lore carries a sense of depth, age, mystery, and reverence. When you use the word "lore," you are suggesting something that has been around for a long time, that belongs to a group of people or a world, and that carries weight and significance. It feels more poetic and weighty than simply saying "information" or "knowledge."

Saying "the lore of the ancient druids" feels rich and mysterious. Saying "the information of the ancient druids" feels flat and clinical. That difference is the spirit of the word.

• Lore is almost always uncountable — you treat it like water or music. You don't say "a lore" or "two lores."
  • You can say "lores" very rarely when contrasting several distinct bodies of knowledge (e.g., "the lores of different cultures"), but this is uncommon.
  • It is commonly paired with words that define whose lore or what lore: local lore, ancient lore, sea lore, woodland lore, dragon lore, the lore of [a fictional world].
  • Common phrases: according to lore, steeped in lore, rich in lore, the lore surrounding..., keeper of the lore.

Lore is the rich, accumulated body of stories, traditions, beliefs, and wisdom that belongs to a culture, community, or world — passed down over time and sitting at the intersection of knowledge, history, and mythology.
